doc.headline: No single configuration meets both gates: the {count.passing.pass_rate|words} reaching {criteria.pass_rate.threshold} in every task exceed {criteria.p95.threshold} p95 overall; only a split of tasks remains open.
doc.lede: With each case in one task, Brisk-S high + retry's overall p95 of {measure.latency_ms.brisk-s.high.r1.p95} puts at least one task over budget, and every configuration inside the budget overall misses the pass-rate gate somewhere. Whether a split clears both, a fast configuration on some tasks and high reasoning on the rest, waits on latency read per task.
doc.flag: Both gates are declared per task, but latency was recorded only over all tasks, so no configuration is shown to pass the latency budget in any task.

caveats.label: Latency read only over all tasks
caveats.material_if: It decides whether a split of tasks is possible: until p95 is read per task, no task-level assignment can be shown to meet the budget. It does not reopen a single configuration unless a case can belong to more than one task, since an overall p95 above {criteria.p95.threshold} otherwise puts at least one task over it.

caveats.label: Task sizes unstated
caveats.material_if: Only where a configuration sits within about a point of the {criteria.pass_rate.threshold} line in a task, since no per-task interval can be read. Many cells do, among them Brisk-S high + retry on multi-hop, Brisk-S low + retry on date math ({criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.datemath.value}) and ambiguous entities ({criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.disamb.value}), Atlas-M high without retry on multi-hop ({criteria.pass_rate.atlas-m.high.r0.multihop.value}), Atlas-M low + retry on multi-hop ({criteria.pass_rate.atlas-m.low.r1.multihop.value}) and Brisk-S high without retry on date math ({criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r0.datemath.value}); the full set is in the gate table. Any of them could fall either side, which changes which configurations a split could use.

It bears on Brisk-S high + retry, picked from {n_candidates|words} configurations and clearing multi-hop by {criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.multihop.gap|abs} points: a rerun on fresh cases tends to read the best of many lower, which would put it below the line there and leave multi-hop without its faster candidate even in a split.

Only for a claim that one configuration beats another: every comparison here is unpaired, so gaps between configurations read wider than paired ones would; no claim on this page rests on separating two of them overall.

decision.text: The pass-rate gate and the latency budget pull opposite ways: the configurations that reach {criteria.pass_rate.threshold} on multi-hop use high reasoning, and high reasoning is what pushes p95 past {criteria.p95.threshold}. The budget is declared per task, but latency was read only over all tasks, so whether a split of tasks clears both cannot be read.

No single configuration clears both gates if each case belongs to one task. Of the two that clear pass rate everywhere, Brisk-S high + retry cost {cost.gap.brisk-s.high.r1.atlas-m.high.r1.per_1k|abs} less per thousand calls than Atlas-M high + retry at this run's serving, whose provider for either model is not named, and their overall pass rates are not told apart. Nano-XS misses the pass-rate gate in all {count.failing.pass_rate.nano-xs.high.r1|words} tasks even at its strongest setting.

Every leg of the split is thin. Read as if each task held its traffic share of the cases, the weakest is Brisk-S low + retry on date math, exactly on the line, so a rerun is as likely to read it below as above ({assumed.share.settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.low.r1.task.datemath.wrong_side}); Brisk-S high + retry clears multi-hop by {criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.multihop.gap|abs} points (below on a rerun {assumed.share.settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.task.multihop.wrong_side} of the time) and ambiguous entities by {criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.disamb.gap|abs} ({assumed.share.settle.criteria.pass_rate.brisk-s.high.r1.task.disamb.wrong_side}). Date math could go to Brisk-S high + retry ({task.datemath.brisk-s.high.r1.pass_rate.mean}) if its latency there allows.

Read p95 per task from this run's traces for Brisk-S low + retry and Brisk-S high + retry, and state each task's case count. A split is open only if Brisk-S high + retry is under budget on multi-hop and ambiguous entities while Brisk-S low + retry is under it on the other tasks.

claims.text: Only Atlas-M high + retry and Brisk-S high + retry reach {criteria.pass_rate.threshold} in all {count.places.pass_rate|words} tasks; multi-hop, {task.multihop.share} of traffic, is the task every other configuration misses.

evidence.caption: Pass rate per task for the six configurations nearest the gate, which is {criteria.pass_rate.threshold} in each task; task sizes are unstated, so no per-task interval is shown.

claims.text: Both run past the {criteria.p95.threshold} budget over all tasks, Brisk-S high + retry at {measure.latency_ms.brisk-s.high.r1.p95} and Atlas-M high + retry at {measure.latency_ms.atlas-m.high.r1.p95}, so each has at least one task over budget; every configuration inside the budget overall misses the pass-rate gate in at least one task.

evidence.caption: Median to p95 latency over all tasks for each configuration, against the per-task budget line.

claims.text: On Brisk-S with retry, high reasoning over low lifts multi-hop by {compare.brisk-s.high.r1.brisk-s.low.r1.pass_rate.task.multihop.difference} points, from {task.multihop.brisk-s.low.r1.pass_rate.mean} below the line to {task.multihop.brisk-s.high.r1.pass_rate.mean} above it, and takes overall p95 from {measure.latency_ms.brisk-s.low.r1.p95} to {measure.latency_ms.brisk-s.high.r1.p95}; overall, the gain is not separated ({compare.brisk-s.high.r1.brisk-s.low.r1.pass_rate.overall.difference} points, interval {compare.brisk-s.high.r1.brisk-s.low.r1.pass_rate.overall.interval}).

The same two configurations' median to p95 latency over all tasks, against the per-task budget line.

claims.text: Brisk-S high + retry is not told apart from Atlas-M high + retry on overall pass rate ({compare.brisk-s.high.r1.atlas-m.high.r1.pass_rate.overall.difference} points, interval {compare.brisk-s.high.r1.atlas-m.high.r1.pass_rate.overall.interval}) and cost {cost.gap.brisk-s.high.r1.atlas-m.high.r1.multiple} as much per thousand calls at this run's serving; the snapshot names no provider for either model, so the ratio is this routing's, not the models'.

evidence.caption: Brisk-S high + retry minus Atlas-M high + retry on pass rate, overall with its unpaired interval and per task as points.

claims.text: Brisk-S low + retry, the fastest configuration near the line, falls short on multi-hop and ambiguous entities and sits exactly on the line on date math; its kept failures are planning errors, a collapsed hop, an off-by-one date window and a missing clarifying question, not malformed output.

evidence.caption: Brisk-S low + retry's pass rate in each task against the {criteria.pass_rate.threshold} gate; with task sizes unstated, its smaller misses could fall either side on a rerun.
The failures kept for Brisk-S low + retry, one per task where it fell short or sat on the line; a sample, not a count.

method.text: {n_candidates|words} configurations: three models crossed with three reasoning levels and retry on or off, each run on {scoreboard.brisk-s.high.r1.cases} cases with none lost; no configuration is a control.

The campaign does not define what makes a task pass; the kept failures compare the planner's calls with an expected plan. The gate is {criteria.pass_rate.threshold} in each of the {count.places.pass_rate|words} tasks, read on the point estimate.

Median and p95 per configuration over all tasks only; the {criteria.p95.threshold} budget is declared per task. An overall p95 above the budget is read as at least one task over it, which assumes each case belongs to one task.

Overall pass-rate differences use each configuration's binomial spread, at the level each block prints, combined as independent and uncorrected for the number of comparisons. Per-task pass rates state no case count and carry no interval; the split's thin legs are sized as if each task held its traffic share of the cases, an assumption labelled as such.
Cost per thousand calls as measured in this run; the provider routing behind each model is not named, so the cost order holds only for this run's serving.

findings.finding: Watch opens with 'Every leg of the split is thin.' The single-lookup leg is not: Brisk-S low + retry reads 98.4%, 1.4 points over the line, and at its traffic-share size would read below it only 0.7% of the time on a rerun. Change it to 'three of the four legs are thin', or name the three legs (date math, multi-hop, ambiguous entities) so the sentence matches the figures that follow it.

items.name: First screen
items.reason: The headline, the decision block and claim quality show that nothing can be picked, explain that the latency budget applies per task, and name the risk that Brisk-S high + retry clears multi-hop by only 0.3 points. The lede then says that reading latency per task 'would show whether one configuration ... can meet both gates'. The page's own confidence line says neither configuration that clears 97% everywhere can be rescued. options_dominance draws the same conclusion: an overall p95 above 600 ms (870 ms and 2551 ms) puts at least one task over the budget. So a reader of the first screen is told a single-configuration answer is still open when it is not. Only a split of tasks is still open.

items.name: Coherent story
items.reason: Each claim matches its values table. Claim quality's rows show only Atlas-M high + retry and Brisk-S high + retry at 97% or above in all four tasks, and every other configuration misses on multi-hop. Claim pair shows -0.7 points, interval -1.7 to +0.4, as the claim says. The inconsistency is page-level. The confidence clause says neither configuration that clears pass rate everywhere can be rescued. The lede, the latency claim ('every configuration is undecided or out') and next step 1 ('whether any single configuration ... can meet the latency budget') treat that as open.

items.name: Honest emphasis
items.reason: The thin 0.3-point clearance on multi-hop is in Watch, and the 37.4% figure is shown under its labelled assumption (it matches settle_cases at 300 assumed cases). The weak spots are elsewhere. Claim pair and the decision block's 'What we know despite it' compare costs (0.18 times as much; $2.84 less) without saying who served each model. Claim levers puts first that low-to-high reasoning with retry 'is not separated overall' (+0.8). It does not say that on multi-hop the same move takes Brisk-S from 95.6% to 97.3%, from missing the gate to clearing it, which is the gap that matters for the decision.

items.name: Sound elision
items.reason: Nothing omitted changes the call. options_dominance agrees that the left-out Atlas-M and Brisk-S configurations, and every Nano-XS configuration, fail pass rate in at least one task. The model effects on Atlas-M and Nano-XS point the same way as on Brisk-S. The snapshot does state a monthly volume (4,000,000), but the page's reason holds: it does not say whether that counts calls or tasks, and cost does not decide this call.

items.name: Confounds handled
items.reason: Four confounds are carried into the story and the next steps: latency read only over all tasks, unstated task sizes, best-of-eighteen selection and no control. The serving provider is handled only in Method. The claims that rank costs do not carry it, so a reader of claim pair takes the 0.18x ratio as a property of the model.

items.name: Actionable next steps
items.reason: Each step names an action and what it would settle: reading per-task p95 and task case counts; declaring whether tasks may be split and which latency line multi-hop is held to; and a multi-hop fix or second retry on Brisk-S low. Step 1 partly asks a question the page's own inference already answers (whether a single configuration can pass), but it is still the step that decides the split.

items.name: Evidence fits claims
items.reason: Claims quality, latency, pair and levers each show their own figures and the gap they describe. Claim failures says Brisk-S low + retry 'misses on multi-hop by 1.4 points and on ambiguous entities by 0.6', but its block holds only three example failures, so neither shortfall is drawn. It also carries no caveat for the unstated task sizes, although a 0.6-point miss could fall either side under any plausible task size. In claim levers, the high-reasoning retry row prints its lower bound as '+0.03535', which is unreadable next to the other one-decimal bounds.

findings.finding: The lede says reading latency per task 'would show whether one configuration, or a split of tasks between two, can meet both gates'. The page's own confidence clause, and code's inferred fact on Atlas-M high + retry, say otherwise. If each case belongs to one task, an overall p95 of 870 ms (Brisk-S high + retry) or 2551 ms (Atlas-M high + retry) puts at least one task over 600 ms. Every other configuration already misses pass rate in some task. So no single configuration meets both gates; only a split of tasks is open. Restate the headline and lede that way, with the condition named (cases split across tasks). Bring the latency claim ('undecided or out') and next step 1 into line: drop 'whether any single configuration ... can meet the latency budget', and drop Atlas-M high + retry from the per-task read unless it is wanted for a split.

Claim pair ('costs 0.18 times as much per thousand calls') and the decision block ('costs $2.84 less per thousand calls ... than Atlas-M high + retry') rank Brisk-S against Atlas-M on cost without naming who served either model. The snapshot does not state the provider or pricing for either arm. Method mentions this, but the claims do not. Name the serving provider for each model in both places, or say there that the provider routing is unstated and the ratio holds only for this run's serving.

Claim levers puts first that low-to-high reasoning with retry is 'not separated overall (+0.8 points)' but costs 357 ms of p95. That reads as if high reasoning buys little. On multi-hop, the same move takes Brisk-S from 95.6% (misses the gate) to 97.3% (clears it), and that is what the call turns on. Add the multi-hop difference (a point estimate, no interval, since task sizes are unstated) to the claim or its block. Also print the high-reasoning retry row's lower bound as +0.04, not +0.03535.

Claim failures says Brisk-S low + retry misses multi-hop by 1.4 points and ambiguous entities by 0.6, but its block draws neither figure, only three examples. Attach the 'Task sizes unstated' caveat to this claim: at the traffic-share size of about 180 ambiguous-entity cases, a 0.6-point miss is well inside a rerun's spread. Either add the two per-task pass rates against the 97% line to the block, or make the sentence about the examples alone.

The confidence clause on unstated task sizes names three near-line cells: Brisk-S high + retry on multi-hop, Atlas-M high without retry on multi-hop at 96.6%, and Brisk-S low + retry on date math at 97%. It leaves out others within about a point that bear on a split: Brisk-S low + retry on ambiguous entities (96.4%), Atlas-M low + retry on multi-hop (96.4%) and Brisk-S high without retry on date math (96.6%). List them, or say the three are examples and not the full set.

items.name: First screen
items.reason: Last round's must_fix is resolved. The headline and lede now say that no single configuration meets both gates and that only a split of tasks is open. They also give the condition: each case belongs to one task. Brisk-S high + retry's 870 ms overall p95 then puts at least one task over 600 ms. The decision block names what would settle the question: per-task p95 for Brisk-S low + retry and Brisk-S high + retry. Claim quality, the first claim, shows why only two configurations are in play. Multi-hop is the task all the others miss, and options_dominance confirms it: every other arm fails the pass-rate gate there, and Atlas-M high + retry is undecided only on latency.

items.name: Coherent story
items.reason: I checked each claim against its block, row by row. In claim quality, only Atlas-M high + retry and Brisk-S high + retry are at or above 97% in all four tasks, and every other row falls below it on multi-hop. In claim latency, every configuration inside 600 ms overall is a Brisk-S or Nano-XS setting that misses pass rate somewhere; Brisk-S low + retry, at 513 ms, misses multi-hop at 95.6%. Claim reasoning (+0.8 overall, interval -0.4 to +2.1; +1.7 on multi-hop) and claim pair (-0.7, interval -1.7 to +0.4) match arms_compare exactly. Claim failures' block now shows 95.6, 97.0 and 96.4 against the 97% line, as its sentence says. Nothing contradicts the headline.

items.name: Honest emphasis
items.reason: Low confidence fits. The confidence clause now lists the near-line cells and points to the gate table for the full set, which resolves last round's finding. The Watch figure checks out: at 300 multi-hop cases, Brisk-S high + retry's 0.3-point clearance would read below the line 37.4% of the time. But Watch names only that one margin. The split the page puts forward also rests on Brisk-S low + retry on date math at exactly 97.0%, with zero margin. It also rests on Brisk-S high + retry on ambiguous entities at +0.6, which would read below the line 29.9% of the time at its traffic-share size of 180 cases. The weakest leg of the split is not in Watch.

items.name: Sound elision
items.reason: Nothing omitted would change the call. Every left-out Atlas-M and Brisk-S configuration fails pass rate in at least one task, as options_dominance shows, so none can serve as a single choice. Nano-XS misses every task. Monthly cost is left out with a stated reason, and the call does not turn on cost. The snapshot holds no figures for outcome mix or extra calls.

items.name: Confounds handled
items.reason: Three confounds are carried into the story and the next steps: latency read only over all tasks, unstated task sizes, and picking the best of many configurations. The cost ranking now says in both places (the decision block and claim pair) that the provider is not named for either model and that the ratio holds only for this run's serving. That resolves last round's must_fix and answers the cost_served_by fact. Missing control is scoped to claim pair, which uses unpaired intervals.

items.name: Actionable next steps
items.reason: Each step names an action and what it would settle. Step one: read per-task p95 for the two Brisk-S settings and record task counts, which settles whether the split meets the budget. Step two: declare whether a split is allowed and which latency line multi-hop is held to. Step three: try a multi-hop decomposition fix or a second retry on Brisk-S low, which tests whether a configuration inside the budget can reach the gate. Last round's finding is resolved: step one no longer asks about single configurations and drops Atlas-M high + retry.

items.name: Evidence fits claims
items.reason: Claim failures' block now draws the per-task pass rates and carries the task-size caveat, which resolves last round's finding. Claim reasoning now shows the +1.7 multi-hop difference, which also resolves last round's finding. Each claim would have to change if its block's values flipped. One small gap: claim reasoning's latency figures (513 ms to 870 ms) appear only in claim latency's block, not in its own.

findings.finding: Watch names only Brisk-S high + retry's 0.3-point clearance on multi-hop. The split the decision block puts forward (Brisk-S high + retry on multi-hop and ambiguous entities, Brisk-S low + retry elsewhere) also depends on Brisk-S low + retry on date math, which sits at exactly 97.0% with no margin, so a rerun is about as likely to land below the line as above it. It also depends on Brisk-S high + retry on ambiguous entities at 97.6%, which would read below the line 29.9% of the time at its traffic-share size of 180 cases. Add the date-math leg to Watch as the split's weakest margin, or say the split could move date math to Brisk-S high + retry (97.9%) if per-task latency allows it.

Claim reasoning says high reasoning 'takes overall p95 from 513 ms to 870 ms', but its block draws only pass-rate differences. Add the two p95 figures to the block or caption, or point the sentence to claim latency's block, so the claim's own trade-off is shown where it is made.

items.name: First screen
items.reason: The headline says no single configuration clears both gates and that only a split of tasks is still open. The decision block says why: the two configurations that reach 97% in every task run past 600 ms p95 overall, and latency was read only over all tasks. It names the main risk, which is thin task-level margins. The first claim, c-quality, shows that multi-hop is the task that separates the configurations. A reader knows what is unresolved and what would settle it.

items.name: Coherent story
items.reason: The claims build on one another. Quality shows who clears 97% per task. Latency shows those two exceed the budget overall and that everyone under budget misses a task. Reasoning shows the trade that causes this. Pair compares the two survivors, and failures shows the fast candidate's misses. I read each sentence against its table. Reasoning's per-task gaps (+0.1, +1.7, +0.9, +1.2) and pair's (-0.7, -0.6, -0.7, -0.7) match the per-task pass rates. Multi-hop passes only for Atlas-M high + retry (97.9%) and Brisk-S high + retry (97.3%), as the quality claim says. Multi-hop as 25% of traffic matches the 300-of-1,200 share. One small overstatement in Watch is noted under findings.

items.name: Honest emphasis
items.reason: Nothing is framed stronger than its interval. The survivors' pass-rate gap is called not told apart (-0.7, interval -1.7 to +0.4). The reasoning gain overall is called not separated (+0.8, -0.4 to +2.1). The thin legs are quantified as labelled assumptions, and the figures check out at traffic-share sizes: 50% on date math, 37.4% on multi-hop and 29.9% on ambiguous entities would read the other way on a rerun. Confidence is Low, and each caveat says what it would change.

items.name: Sound elision
items.reason: Everything left out is sound. Options dominance with gates confirms that every configuration other than the two high + retry ones fails pass rate in at least one task, so the cut configurations, Nano-XS and the lever detail cannot change the call. Outcome mix and extra calls have no figures in the snapshot. Monthly cost does not bear on a call that turns on gates.

items.name: Confounds handled
items.reason: Latency read only overall is carried into the headline, decision, claim latency, Method and the first next step. The page also states the logic that an overall p95 above 600 ms means some task is over, and the condition it rests on: each case belongs to one task. Unstated task sizes are carried as a labelled traffic-share assumption. Best-of-many is tied to the 0.3-point multi-hop margin. The unnamed provider is stated wherever cost is compared, which answers the cost_served_by fact.

items.name: Actionable next steps
items.reason: Each step names an action and what it settles. Reading per-task p95 and case counts for the two Brisk-S configurations settles whether the split meets the budget and whether each leg is borderline. Declaring whether tasks may be split, and which latency line multi-hop is held to, settles whether a split is a valid option. Running a decomposition fix or a second retry on low-reasoning Brisk-S settles whether a configuration under budget can reach 97% on the two tasks it misses.

The examples match the snapshot, and the one malformed-output example belongs to Nano-XS, as the claim implies. If the per-task values flipped, the claims would have to change.
